messages.subject: set_capacity does not accept function
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Does set_capacity() within a trajectory not accept a function for its resource parameter?

I currently have the following code to check the current mean queue size and call set_capacity if a threshold is reached.

s1.current <- 1

update_current <- function() {
  s1.current <<- s1.current + 1
  return(0)
}

t_scale <- trajectory("Scale") %>%
  branch(option = function() { (mean(get_queue_count(env, paste0("s1_", s1.current))) > config$s1.scaler.threshold) }, continue = F,
         trajectory() %>%
           timeout(function() update_current()) %>%
           set_capacity(function() {paste0("s1_", s1.current)}, value = config$s1.capacity) %>%
           log_(function() {paste0("Added new s1 resource. ", s1.current)})) %>%
  log_("No resources added.")

The idea is to keep track of resources that currently have a capacity > 0 within s1.current. Everytime the threshold is reached, the timeout activity calls the update_current function that increases s1.current by one.

However, set_capacity does not accept the function as its argument and fails with. Without the function i run into the problem that the expression is evaluated during definition instead of runtime.

Error: set_capacity: 'resource' is not a valid character

I tried the same using a global attribute instead of a base R variable but got the same error.

What would be the right way to achieve this? Specifically, how do i dynamically change the capacity of a resource of which i have to assembly the name at runtime?

It does not.

> What would be the right way to achieve this? Specifically, how do i dynamically change the capacity of a resource of which i have to assembly the name at runtime?

TL;DR, use "select" and then "set_capacity_selected".

Long explanation follows. Resources are special, because a "unit of
interaction" typically spans over several activities. Consider the
following:

seize("something") %>%
timeout(t) %>%
release("something")

If we allow "something" to be a function, then something may change
during the course of that timeout and your trajectory becomes invalid
because you are selecting a different resource for releasing. To avoid
this kind of mistakes, every activity that deals with resources has
its *_selected() counterpart that acts on the resource selected by the
select() activity. Thus, this is equivalent to the example above:

select("something") %>%
seize_selected() %>%
timeout(t) %>%
release_selected()

And now "something" can be substituted by a function, and no matter
what happens, the trajectory integrity is preserved.

Regards,
--

On Wed, 22 Jul 2020 at 23:46, Sam Schaffel <sam.sch...@gmail.com> wrote:

This is the main issue: there are two "simultaneous" (because there is
no timeout between them) send() activities. This typically leads to
undefined behaviour, because it's impossible to order the events
properly anymore.

More specifically, the second consecutive send() is triggering a
secondary handler when the arrivals didn't reach the
timeout_from_attribute yet, and thus they end up executing *two*
timeouts instead of one.

TL;DR, the send() activity between resources is superfluous, and the
solution is to remove it, as you found.

Actually, on second thought, if the number of arrivals in resource 1
is going to affect the timeout too, it's not superfluous anymore,
because as soon as resource 2 is full, the arrival will end up in its
queue without executing any send()...

So the most general solution is to insert timeout(0) after the first
send() and before seizing the second resource. The timeout() activity
has the lowest priority, so even a null timeout effectively splits up
a simultaneous event chain.
